title: Inverness Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Inverness well records show a 290 ft median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and typical finished-well costs of $20,500-$32,300.
h1: What to Know About Wells in Inverness, Colorado
intro_html: Buying land or a home in Inverness means looking beyond the listing’s statement that a property has a well. Colorado DWR records show 4,248 permitted wells within 5 miles, but only 1,903 are recorded as constructed, 2,244 report total depth, 930 report pump yield, and 126 report a static water level. Those gaps matter. The nearby record gives useful local ranges for depth, production, water level, and cost, but a permit search is not a substitute for inspecting the specific well, pump, pressure system, water quality, and septic layout.

sections.heading: Inverness well depth reflects Denver Basin ground
sections.html:
The median reported well depth around Inverness is 290 feet. The middle half runs from 54 to 477 feet, so a driller’s bid based only on the median can miss the conditions on a particular lot. Seventeen percent of reported wells are 600 feet or deeper, while 33% are under 100 feet, 18% fall from 100 to 300 feet, and 32% from 300 to 600 feet.

The drilling model identifies Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, with Denver Basin aquifer wells making up 100% of named aquifer records. Permits also identify 1,997 wells in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, 650 in the Denver aquifer, and 466 in Lower Dawson. Nearby Centennial, Dove Valley, Meridian, and Lone Tree can provide comparison records, but your parcel still controls the final depth.

sections.heading: A 15 gpm median is a useful local production benchmark
sections.html:
Among the 930 wells that report pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 12.0 to 15.0 gpm. Half of reported wells produce from 5 to 15 gpm, and half produce more than 15 gpm. No reported wells fall under 1 gpm or from 1 to 5 gpm in this dataset.

That is a stronger production profile than many Colorado locations, but it is not a guarantee for an untested well. Yield tests measure a particular well and aquifer, not every lot in Inverness. Confirm the well’s permitted use, pump setting, pressure tank performance, and recovery. Household, stock, and irrigation uses make up 42%, 7%, and 6% of the recorded use mix, while monitoring wells account for 25%.

sections.heading: Water levels vary widely, so the decade figures need context
sections.html:
The reported static water level has a median depth of 172 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 51 to 519 feet. That spread is large enough to affect pump selection, electrical planning, and the cost of reaching the water level. A well’s static level should be measured after the well has rested, not assumed from a nearby permit.

The decade medians are 150 feet in the 1970s, 404 feet in the 1980s, 931 feet in the 2000s, 253 feet in the 2010s, and 145 feet in the 2020s. This does not show a simple continuing decline. The records are uneven, with only 126 wells reporting a static water level, and measurements may represent different locations and conditions. Treat the series as historical context, not a parcel-specific forecast.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long use around Inverness
sections.html:
Permit activity began in the 1950s, with 83 permits issued then and 95 in the 1960s. Activity increased to 635 permits in the 1970s, 620 in the 1980s, 761 in the 1990s, and 598 in the 2000s. The record shows 370 permits in the 2010s and 226 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active drillers in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 618 wells; Hier Drilling Co Inc (Hier, Bruce A.), with 470; and Hier Drilling Co. (Hier, Peter J), with 332. These counts describe permit records, not current availability or an endorsement. Check the original permit, construction report, abandonment record, and any later well-test paperwork before relying on a historical driller entry.

sections.heading: What drilling a well costs near Inverness
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses $50-$70 per foot for Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 290-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $14,500-$20,300. That is only the hole. A finished well including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $20,500-$32,300.

The 54-to-477-foot middle range explains why bids can vary substantially from one parcel to another. A well near the 90th-percentile depth of 1,297 feet would be a very different project from a shallow hole, and the deepest record is 2,485 feet. Ask each contractor what depth is included, what happens if the hole is dry or low-producing, and which pump, tank, trenching, electrical, casing, and grout items are included.

sections.heading: Inverness buyers should investigate water quality and site limits
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information deserves a close review before closing. Within about 10 miles are 224 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 5 historic mine features, and 20 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped locations do not prove that a specific well is contaminated, but they are a reason to test the property’s water and check the site history, groundwater direction, and any required cleanup information.

Low yield and dry holes remain site-specific risks even with a 15.0 gpm reported median. Confirm the well construction, casing, grout, pump, static level, and recovery test. Also verify that the septic system and replacement area fit the lot, and that the well location works with the home, access, setbacks, drainage, and future building plans. A permit for household use does not automatically solve every water-rights or land-use question.

sections.heading: Use the nearby record to plan a parcel-specific decision
sections.html:
For a purchase in Inverness, start with the exact well permit and construction report, then compare nearby records in Centennial, Dove Valley, Acres Green, Meridian, Cherry Creek, and Lone Tree. The goal is not to find one average number; it is to see whether the parcel’s depth, aquifer name, yield, and static level fit the surrounding pattern.

Have a qualified contractor inspect the well and pressure system, and obtain a current water test before removing inspection conditions. If you plan to build, confirm the permitted use and any augmentation or water-rights requirements that apply to the basin and proposed use. Price the complete project rather than drilling alone, and keep contingency room for deeper drilling, a larger pump, trenching, electrical work, septic construction, and site access.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Inverness, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Inverness is 290 feet. The middle half runs from 54 to 477 feet. About 33% are under 100 feet, while 17% are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest recorded well is 2,485 feet, so a nearby well is useful for comparison but cannot set your parcel’s final depth.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Inverness?
faq.a: The drilling model uses $50-$70 per foot. At the local median depth of 290 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at $14,500-$20,300. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $20,500-$32,300. A deeper-than-typical well, difficult access, or added site work can change the contractor’s bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Inverness?
faq.a: Among 930 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 12.0 to 15.0 gpm. Half report 5 to 15 gpm and half report more than 15 gpm. Those figures describe tested records, not a guarantee. Review the property’s own yield and recovery test before buying.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Inverness?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that water is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapping shows 224 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 5 historic mine features, and 20 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well through a qualified laboratory and review the site history. Nearby mapped sites are a reason to investigate, not proof of contamination.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping near Inverness?
faq.a: The reported static-water medians are 150 feet below surface in the 1970s, 404 feet in the 1980s, 931 feet in the 2000s, 253 feet in the 2010s, and 145 feet in the 2020s. That does not show a simple continuing decline. Only 126 wells report static levels, and the measurements may represent different locations and conditions.
